title: The poet's question
hookLine: the monk-poet Vangisa asks what became of his teacher who has died

cards: When someone who taught you dies, a strange question can rise up, one you might not say out loud. Where are they now? Did they get where they were going?
Were they at peace? Among the Buddha's monks was Vangisa, a wandering poet before he ordained. Words came to him fast, in verse, and the Buddha praised him for it.
Now his own teacher, an elder named Nigrodhakappa, has died. Vangisa sits alone, and the question comes. He doesn't keep it to himself.

teach.h: A POET'S PRAISE, LIKE A LETTER
teach.b: Vangisa goes to the Buddha and asks, as a poet would, in verse. He opens with praise, the way you'd open a letter to someone you love.
You who cut through doubts, he says, a monk has died here, known and honored, peaceful. Then the real question.
Was my teacher fully freed, or did something still bind him? Did he cross over, or is there more to his journey? All of us here, he says, want to hear it.

It's a brave question, the kind that can go unasked for fear of the answer. The Buddha's answer is short. He cut off craving for this world of name and form, the stream that had run in him for a long time.
He crossed over birth and death completely. And Vangisa's joy pours out in more verses. My question wasn't wasted, he says.
I wasn't let down. Notice two things.
First, the poem lets trust and an open question sit in the same person: Vangisa trusts the teaching, and he still needs to ask.
Second, his love for his teacher comes out as art. At a funeral, words can run out. Vangisa's didn't.
He gave them to his teacher, asking out loud what everyone around him wanted to know.

how: Buddhists remember teachers who have died with memorial offerings, chanting and merit dedications, and many monasteries keep the death anniversaries of their teachers.

o: the monk-poet who asked if his teacher was freed
a king who asked the Buddha about rebirth
the elder teacher who had just died

games.q: the poet's question: tap the pairs.
p: a monk who had been a wandering poet

s: Vangisa asks his question in verse
he opens with praise, then asks whether his teacher was fully freed.
in this poem the Buddha won't say what became of the teacher
here he answers: the teacher cut off craving and crossed birth and death.
Vangisa had been a poet before he became a monk
words came to him fast, and the Buddha praised his gift.

games.q: you're Vangisa. your teacher has died, and you wonder whether he was fully freed. what do you do?
o: decide the answer on your own.
games.why: he goes to the Buddha and asks in verse, and the Buddha answers that his teacher crossed birth and death.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something that lasted: a parent, a coach, a teacher, a grandparent, living or gone, and see their face clearly.
Ask what they gave you, and let one true sentence form, with no need for it to be perfect. Say it silently to them, the way Vangisa might, then rest.

wordCard.voice: Vangisa. The monk-poet, grieving his teacher, asking the Buddha in verse whether he was freed, and turning his love into words.

orig.note: Pali Vangisa: the monk-poet, praised in the texts for his gift of ready inspiration.

carryVoice: Your line: my question wasn't wasted. Trust and a question can live in the same heart. Thanks for sitting with me.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1, Etadaggavagga: Vangisa foremost in ready inspiration (patibhana)
